Research Paper 
Effect of nanobubble water on medium chain carboxylic acids production in 
anaerobic digestion of cow manure 
Yang Liu a,b,c, Xiaomei Ye a,b, Kequan Chen c, Xiayuan Wu c, Lihua Jiao a,b, Hongyu Zhang a,b, 
Fei Zhu a,b, Yonglan Xi a,b,d,* 
a Jiangsu Academy of Agriculture Sciences, Nanjing 210014, China 
b Key Laboratory of Crop and Livestock Integration, Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, Jiangsu Collaborative Innovation Center for Solid Organic Waste Resource 
Utilization, 210014 Nanjing, China 
c State Key Laboratory of Materials-Oriented Chemical Engineering, College of Biotechnology and Pharmaceutical, Nanjing Tech University, Nanjing 210009, China 
d Department of Applied Ecology, Faculty of Environmental Sciences, Czech University of Life Sciences Prague, Kamýcka 129, Praha-Suchdol 16500, Czech Republic   
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Anaerobic digestion 
Chain elongation 
Nanobubble water 
Electron transport 
Fatty acid cycle pathway 
A B S T R A C T   
Nanobubble water promotes the degradation of difficult-to-degrade organic matter, improves the activity of 
electron transfer systems during anaerobic digestion, and optimizes the composition of anaerobic microbial 
communities. Therefore, this study proposes the use of nanobubble water to improve the yield of medium chain 
carboxylic acids produced from cow manure by chain elongation. The experiment was divided into two stages: 
the first stage involved the acidification of cow manure to produce volatile acidic fatty acids as electron ac­
ceptors, and the second phase involved the addition of lactic acid as an electron donor for the chain elongation. 
Three experimental groups were established, and air, H2, and N2 nanobubble water were added in the second 
stage. Equal amounts of deionized water were added in the control group. The results showed that nanobubble 
water supplemented with air significantly increased the caproic acid concentration to 15.10 g/L, which was 
55.03 % greater than that of the control group. The relative abundances of Bacillus and Caproiciproducens, which 
are involved in chain elongation, and Syntrophomonas, which is involved in electron transfer, increased. The 
unique ability of air nanobubble water supplemented to break down the cellulose matrix resulted in further 
decomposition of the recalcitrant material in cow manure. This effect subsequently increased the number of 
microorganisms associated with lignocellulose degradation, increasing carbohydrate metabolism and ATP- 
binding cassette transporter protein activity and enhancing fatty acid cycling pathways during chain elonga­
tion. Ultimately, this approach enabled the efficient production of medium chain carboxylic acids.   
1. Introduction 
The rapidly growing population has significantly increased milk and 
beef consumption, leading to the production of approximately 7.6 
million tons of cow manure per year worldwide (Boldú and Pous, 2020; 
Jomnonkhaow et al., 2021). As biomass resources, organic waste such as 
cow manure can be converted into organic fertilizers, bioenergy and 
high value-added chemicals (Kunatsa and Xia, 2022). Cow manure is 
suitable as a substrate for anaerobic digestion (AD) due to its high 
moisture, high ash content, high lignocellulose content, abundance of 
alkali metals and AD microorganisms (Li et al., 2021). It has been 
confirmed that animal manure can generate medium chain carboxylic 
acids (MCCAs) through AD, with caproic acid being its primary product. 
Zhang et al. used swine manure as substrate and added ethanol as an 
electron donor for AD to produce MCCAs. As a result, the concentration 
of caproic acid reached 3.9 g/L (Zhang et al., 2020). Lian et al. found 
that the co-digestion of corn straw and cow manure to produce lactic 
acid at medium temperature simultaneously produced caproic acid, and 
the percentage of caproic acid could be 7.19–14.06 % (Lian et al., 2022). 
MCCAs are carboxylic acid molecules with 6–12 carbon atoms. It is a 
significant organic molecule that can be employed as an antibacterial 
agent, food additive, precursor of liquid biofuels, and growth-promoting 
antibiotic alternative in animal feed (Contreras-D´avila et al., 2021). 
Therefore, converting organic matter such as animal manure into 
MCCAs through AD can not only process waste and protect the envi­
ronment, but also have high economic returns.

The chain elongation (CE) reaction is the main process used to pro­
duce MCCAs by AD. The process uses ethanol or lactic acid as the 
electron donor and volatile fatty acids (VFAs) as the electron acceptor, 
and an electron donor is used to increase the length of the carbon chain 
of the electron acceptor to achieve the production of MCCAs (Wu et al., 
2019a). Therefore, electron donors and acceptors are indispensable 
prerequisites for MCCAs production in AD. The Gibbs free energy values 
for the CE reaction using lactic acid and ethanol as an electron donors 
were −123.1 kJ/mol and −79.0 kJ/mol, respectively, and lactic acid has 
thermodynamic advantages over ethanol when used as an electron 
donor (Zhang et al., 2022b). By introducing lactic acid bacteria into 
waste that is high in carbohydrates, lactic acid can be generated, which 
makes the process more advantageous both ecologically and economi­
cally (Kang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022b). For these reasons, CE 
reactions driven by lactic acid as an electron donor have received much 
attention in recent years. However, inefficiencies arise in the synthesis of 
MCCAs due to challenges such as low electron transfer efficiency, 
restricted substrate utilization by CE microorganisms, and competitive 
metabolism (Wu et al., 2019a; Wu et al., 2021b). If the rate-limiting 
process mentioned above can be increased during AD, MCCAs yield 
will be further improved. 
Nanobubble is defined as bubbles less than 1000 nm in diameter. It 
has unique physical and chemical properties, such as a high negative 
Zeta potential, stability, and solubility, and generates reactive oxygen 
species (Chuenchart et al., 2021). Nanobubbles have a high-curvature 
gas-liquid interface, which has a very high surface energy and can 
therefore adsorb and aggregate microbial cells (Zhang et al., 2022c). 
Nanobubble water (NBW) has been investigated in AD biogas produc­
tion and has shown good performance in promoting the degradation of 
lignocellulose, increasing the activity of the electron transport system 
(ETS), and optimizing the microbial community structure (Wang et al., 
2020a; Wang et al., 2020b). For example, wang et al. investigated the 
effect of O2-containing gas NBW on cellulose AD and showed that the 
addition of NBW reduced cellulose content and cellulose crystallinity by 
8–14 % and 9–21 %, respectively, and ETS activity by 1.7-fold (Wang 
et al., 2020b). For example, Wang et al. reported that CO-NBW increased 
the methane production rate by 21.4 %, improved substrate degrada­
tion, enriched methanogenic bacteria, and optimized the composition of 
the microbial community (Wang et al., 2023b). The CE process depends 
on CE bacteria. CE bacteria are also anaerobic bacteria that coexist and 
cooperate with hydrolyzing and acidifying bacteria (Wang et al., 
2023e). Hence, it will be intriguing to determine whether NBW enhance 
the degradation of recalcitrant organic matter, improve electron transfer 
efficiency, and optimize the microbial community structure in MCCAs 
producing systems. To our knowledge, this is the first time that the effect 
of NBW on MCCAs production performance has been evaluated. 
Therefore, this research aimed to elucidate the effect of different 
types of NBW (air, H2 and N2) on the production of MCCAs from cow 
manure AD. The AD experiment comprised two stages: 1) The first stage 
was an acidification experiment where electron acceptor VFAs were 
produced from cow manure AD. 2) The second stage was a CE experi­
ment where an exogenous electron donor (lactic acid) was added to the 
first-stage products to produce MCCAs. NBW was added in the second 
stage to assess the effect of NBW on MCCAs synthesis. Then, the effects 
of the properties of NBW, such as negative Zeta potential, release of 
reactive oxygen species, high stability, and high mass transfer efficiency, 
on substrate degradation, intermediate product production, electron 
transfer efficiency, key enzyme activities and anaerobic microbial 
community structure in the AD process were investigated to explore the 
mechanism of action of NBW. This research contributes to the devel­
opment of sustainable solutions to increase the production of high value- 
added products from biomass resources. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Substrates and inoculums 
Cow manure was obtained from Zhongxin Dairy Farming Profes­
sional Cooperative, Xinghua City, Jiangsu Province, China. The samples 
were stored at −20 ◦C. The inoculum for acidification was collected from 
the Taihu New City Wastewater Treatment Plant, Wuxi City, Jiangsu 
Province, China. The samples were subjected to heat shock treatment at 
75 ◦C for 3 h to inhibit the activity of methanogenic bacteria (Arslan 
et al., 2016). The inoculum for CE was collected from the running CE 
reactor in the laboratory. During reactor operation, cow manure is 
employed as the substrate, exogenous lactic acid serves as the electron 
donor, and caproic acid is the primary product. The physical and 
chemical indicators of the inoculum and cow manure are shown in 
Table S1. 
2.2. Preparation of NBW 
NBW was prepared using a nanobubble generator (Shanghai 
Zhongjing Environmental Protection Technology Co., Ltd., ZJC-NM, 
China), where deionized water and gas (air, H2, and N2) were fed into 
(150 mL/min) the nanobubble generator (Fig. 1). 
2.3. AD experimental setup 
2.3.1. Acidification of cow manure 
First, 143 g of cow manure, 30 g of inoculum used for acidification, 
and 277 g of deionized water were added to a 500-mL glass serum bottle 
and mixed thoroughly. The pH in the glass serum bottle was adjusted to 
6.5 ± 0.1 with 5 M HCl and NaOH, after which the glass serum bottle 
was sealed. The cap of the bottle had two holes to connect the silicone 
tubes for sampling during fermentation. After sealing, the headspace 
portion of the glass serum bottle was purged with pure nitrogen for 10 
min to expel the air inside the bottle and create an anaerobic 
environment. 
2.3.2. CE experimental setup 
When lactic acid acts as an electron donor, the CE process includes 
two metabolic pathways, including reverse β oxidation (RBO) and fatty

acid cycling (FAB), as shown in Fig. 2. The fermentation substrate for the 
CE experiment was the digest produced in Section 2.3.1. To ensure that 
the fermentation substrate was the same for the different treatment 
groups, all the acidified fermentation products generated in Section 
2.3.1 were mixed together and stirred well. Then, 250 mL of the mixture 
was taken and added to 500-mL glass serum bottles for the CE experi­
ments. The inoculum for the CE experiments was obtained from the 
running CE reactor, and 50 mL was added to each glass serum bottle. 
Then, 100 mL of NBW or deionized water. The three experimental 
groups were Air-NBW, H2-NBW and N2-NBW, which were named Air, H2 
and N2, respectively, and deionized water served as the control group, 
which was named CK. Three replicates were used for each experimental 
group. The lactic acid/VFAs ratio was set to 3. VFAs were derived from 
the fermentation of cow manure produced during the acidification 
phase, and the initial VFAs concentrations in the glass serum bottles was 
9.83 ± 0.21 g/L. Therefore, 11.8 g of lactate was added to each glass 
serum vial, resulting in a final lactate concentration of 29.5 ± 0.12 g/L. 
The pH inside the glass serum vials was then adjusted to 5.5 ± 0.1 with 
5 M NaOH. The caps were tightly screwed on, and the tops of the glass 
serum vials were emptied and purged with nitrogen gas for 10 min to 
create an anaerobic environment. The glass serum vials for the CE ex­
periments were placed in a water bath (30 ± 1 ◦C) for 18 days (see 
Table 1). The selection of these three gases for NBW preparation is based 
on the following considerations. Air is cost effective and readily avail­
able without the need for purchase, and previous studies have indicated 
that a microaerobic environment can enhance AD (Cao et al., 2022). 
Exogenous supplementation of hydrogen gas improves electron transfer 
efficiency and increase MCCAs production (Wu et al., 2019b); thus, it is 
important to investigate the effects of NBW prepared with hydrogen gas. 
Nitrogen gas is commonly used to create anaerobic environments, and 
nitrogen gas NBW contributes to the enhancement of AD performance 
and lignocellulose degradation (Yang et al., 2020). 
Liquid samples were collected every two days for the determination 
of pH, VFAs, lactic acid, ammonia nitrogen, and MCCAs concentrations. 
After AD, the degasification mixture samples were subjected to extra­
cellular polymeric substance (EPS), LDH, oxidation reduction potential 
(ORP), cyclic voltammetry (CV), ETS, electron accept capacity (EAC), 
electron doner capacity (EDC), electrochemical impedance spectroscopy 
(EIS), I–t, and microbial community composition analyses. The biogas 
residue was freeze–vacuum dried, and substrate degradation was char­
acterized using X-ray diffraction (XRD), X-ray photoelectron spectros­
copy (XPS), and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR). The 
biogas slurry was filtered through a 0.45-μm filter membrane, and the 
filtered solution was dissolved organic matter (DOM). XRD, FTIR and 
EEM were used to characterize the DOM to analyze whether more 
substrates were converted into DOM. 
2.4. Analytical methods 
For the detection of MCCAs using gas chromatography (GC-2030, 
Shimadzu), a gas chromatograph was used. The temperatures of the 
injector and detector were 275 and 300 ◦C, respectively, and the 
capillary column temperature was increased from 70 to 170 ◦C at 20 ◦C/ 
min and increased to 240 ◦C at 20 ◦C/min after 5 min. Lactic acid was 
detected using high-performance liquid chromatography (LC-1260, 
Agilent) on an HSS T3 column (4.61 × 150 mm, 5 μm, Waters) with a 
mobile phase of 20 mM sodium dihydrogen phosphate (pH 2.7), an in­
jection volume of 10 μL, a detection wavelength of 210 nm, and a col­
umn temperature of 30 ◦C. 
Total solids (TS), volatile solids (VS), pH, CV, EIS, ORP, XRD, total 
carbon and total nitrogen content, ammonia nitrogen concentration, and 
VFAs concentration were determined as reported in our previously 
published article (Liu et al., 2022). The I–t curve was measured at 
constant voltage for 5 min at +0.6 V (positive potential) and −0.6 V 
(negative potential) (He et al., 2014). The methods used for EAC and 
EDC detection are described in the literature (He et al., 2014). The 
different fractions of EPS, such as loose-bound EPS (LBEPS) and tight- 
bound EPS (TBEPS), were extracted following previously reported 
methods (Wu et al., 2021c; Yang et al., 2019). Lactate dehydrogenase 
(LDH) was measured using an LDH kit (Solarbio, China). ETS activity 
was determined using the INT assay (Hou et al., 2022). Microbial 
community analysis was conducted using high-throughput sequencing 
of 16S rRNA, and the PCR amplification primer 515F-806R was selected. 
GENE DENOVO was commissioned to perform high-throughput

XPS was performed with a Thermo Scientific K-Alpha+, and EEM

The FTIR test wavelength ranged from 400 to 4000 cm−1. The Zeta 
potential was tested using a nanoparticle size potentiometer (NICOMP 
Z3000, USA). 
2.5. Data analysis 
For analysis, the experimental data were fed into SPSS 26.0 
(Microsoft, USA), while OriginPro 2023b (Origin Lab, USA) was used to 
generate figures. During the CE experiment, liquid samples were 
collected from the experimental facility every two days to detect the 
concentrations of MCCAs and VFAs. In order to ensure the reliability and 
accuracy of the experimental results, we prepared three glass serum 
vials for each experimental group as repeat samples, so three sets of data 
will be obtained for each sample. Subsequently, we imported these data 
into SPSS 26.0 statistical software for in-depth analysis. By performing 
the single-factor ANOVA test, we were able to calculate the p-value of 
the difference significance between the different groups to determine 
whether there was a statistically significant difference between the 
groups. In order to understand more precisely which experimental

3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Impact of nanobubble water on MCCAs production from cow manure 
To investigate the influence of various types of NBW on the pro­
duction of MCCAs, distinct experimental groups were established using 
air, H2, and N2. As shown in Fig. 3, significant variance in the concen­
trations of MCCAs (specifically caproic acid, heptanoic acid, and cap­
rylic acid) were noted among these three types of NBW. For the initial 6 
days of AD, the MCCAs concentrations in each experimental group 
exhibited minor fluctuations between 2 and 4 g/L, devoid of obvious 
alterations. However, the MCCAs concentrations of the Air experimental 
groups increased notably on the 8th day of the experiment, peaking on 
the 12th day. The peak concentrations of caproic acid, heptanoic acid, 
and caprylic acid were 15.10, 1.82, and 0.51 g/L, respectively. The peak 
concentrations of caproic acid, heptanoic acid, and caprylic acid in the 
Air experimental group were 55.03, 62.50, and 131.82 % greater than 
those in the CK experimental group (9.74, 1.12, and 0.22 g/L, respec­
tively). Tukey HSD analysis revealed that considering 95 % confidence 
intervals, the MCCAs concentrations in the Air experimental group were 
significantly greater than those in the CK experimental group (p < 0.05). 
An increase in the concentrations of MCCAs of more than 50 % indicates 
that air-NBW has a significant effect on MCCAs production. The H2 
experimental group reached peak concentrations of 9.47, 1.01, and 0.20 
g/L for caproic acid, heptanoic acid, and caprylic acid, respectively. 
9.15, 1.08, and 0.19 g/L for caproic, heptanoic, and caprylic acids, 
respectively, in the N2 experimental group. The concentration of caproic 
acid in the H2 experimental group did not significantly differ from that 
in the CK experimental group (p = 0.358). Moreover, the concentrations 
of heptanoic acid and caprylic acid were significantly lower than those 
in the CK group (p < 0.05). The concentration of caproic acid was 
significantly lower in the N2 experimental group than in the CK exper­
imental group (p < 0.05). The concentration of heptanoic acid did not 
significantly differ from that in the CK experimental group (p > 0.05). 
The concentration of caprylic acid was also significantly lower than that 
in the CK experimental group (p < 0.05). The main component of the 
MCCAs in each experimental group was caproic acid, and air-NBW had a 
significant promoting effect on caproic acid. 
Different types of NBW exhibited different effects in comparison to 
those in the CK experimental group. The concentrations of MCCAs in the 
Air experimental group increased most significantly from 6 to 12 days. 
The variation in the impact of NBW type on MCCAs synthesis was 
potentially attributed to the gas type of the NBW species since the same 
preparation process for NBW was employed in this study, except for the 
difference in gas type. The concentration of caproic acid used in this 
study is notable. For instance, Zhang et al. reported that the highest 
concentration of caproic acid in their investigation of MCCAs production 
from swine manure AD was 3.9 g/L (Zhang et al., 2020). The concen­
tration of caproic acid reached a high level (15.10 g/L) in this study 
compared with previous studies. Wang et al. investigated the impact of 
nanobubble water on AD and found that nanobubbles enhance microbial 
activity by promoting ATP synthesis. Moreover, the use of oxygenated 
nanobubble water led to a boost in the electron transfer efficiency of the 
AD system (Wang et al., 2020b). ETS activity in the AD system reflects 
the respiratory activity of anaerobic microorganisms (Wang et al., 
2022). Deng et al. showed a significant positive correlation between 
caproic acid yield and ETS activity (Deng et al., 2024). Therefore, the 
highest levels of MCCAs in the Air experimental group may be related to 
microbial activity, which specifically needs to be analyzed in terms of 
microbial community structure. 
3.2. Effect of nanobubble water on key physicochemical factors 
Fig. S1a-B shows that the bubble sizes in the three NBWs are mainly 
between 100 and 600 nm. The bubble concentration in different NBWs 
at 200 nm is the highest compared to other sizes. The total nanobubble 
concentration was the highest for Air-NBW followed by N2-NBW, and 
the lowest concentration was noted for H2-NBW. Fig. S1c-e shows the 
nanobubble Brownian motion images, demonstrating that the water 
samples with different NBWs contained nanobubbles. NTA revealed the 
successful preparation of different types of NBW with different con­
centrations and sizes. The Zeta potential of Air-NBW was −13.83 ± 0.26 
mV, that of H2-NBW was −9.03 ± 0.63 mV, and that of N2-NBW was 
−15.13 ± 0.30 mV. Significant differences in the Zeta potentials of the 
three types of NBWs were noted (p < 0.05). The Air experimental group 
had the highest concentration of smaller nanobubbles and the highest 
concentration of caproic acid. The change in the concentration of cap­
roic acid may be related to these properties. VFAs are the electron ac­
ceptors of the CE process and undergo carbon chain lengthening by 
reacting with acetyl coenzyme A generated by the oxidation of electron 
donors, yielding two carbon atoms each cycle (Wu et al., 2021a). Thus, 
the CE process entails the conversion of acetic acid to butyric acid, 
butyric acid to caproic acid, caproic acid to octanoic acid (even carbon), 
and propionic acid to valeric acid, followed by the conversion of valeric 
acid to heptanoic acid (odd carbon). As shown in Fig. 4 a–d, on the 12th 
day of the experiment, the butyric acid concentration in the Air exper­
imental group was 2.03 g/L, which was significantly lower than the 
4.00 g/L in the CK experimental group (p < 0.05). The valeric acid 
concentration in the Air experimental group was 1.58 g/L, which was 
significantly lower than the 2.60 g/L in the CK experimental group (p <
0.05). This change indicated that the CE reaction could quickly syn­
thesize MCCAs in the Air experimental group. In addition, butyric acid 
and valerate concentrations were lower in the air group compared with 
the other groups after the CE reaction began, indicating that the CE 
reaction rate was faster. In addition, the precursors (butyric acid and 
valerate acid) to the synthesis of MCCAs were rapidly consumed, so the 
concentrations were lower. We also observed that the propionic acid 
concentration in the air experimental group was lower than that in the 
other groups. When lactic acid serves as the electron donor, propionic 
acid is produced as a byproduct through the propionate pathway 
(Fig. 1), forming a competitive relationship with the MCCAs metabolic 
pathway (Ma et al., 2022). The addition of Air-NBW may influence the 
microbial community structure, weakening the competitive pathway of 
propionic acid, and allowing more lactic acid to be utilized for MCCAs 
production. 
Lactic acid serves as an electron donor for the CE reaction, so the 
consumption of lactic acid reflects CE reaction progression. As shown in 
Fig. 4e, lactic acid depleted faster in the air experimental group than in 
the CK experimental group, with a concentration of only 1.07 g/L by Day 
8. By Day 10, the lactic acid level was 0.05 g/L, indicating that the 
addition of Air-NBW led to earlier consumption of the electron donor 
and accelerated the carboxylate platform fermentation process. The 
experimental group exposed to H2 showed a reduction in lactic acid to 
17.52 g/L on Day 8, which continued to decrease to 0.03 g/L on Day 10. 
The lactic acid concentration changes in the N2 and CK experimental 
groups were similar; they began to decrease on the 10th day and reached 
0 g/L by the 12th day. The Air experimental group displayed a signifi­
cant increase in the MCCAs concentrations, indicating that Air-NBW 
accelerated the conversion of lactic acid to acetyl coenzyme A, 
thereby accelerating the CE reaction. The increase in the concentrations 
of MCCAs is potentially related to the improvement in electron transport 
efficiency and the optimization of the microbial community structure in 
the AD system. 
In the MCCAs production process, pH is a key index used to represent 
the stability of the AD system. The pH changes exhibited by each 
experimental group during AD are shown in Fig. 4f. During the initial 6 
days of fermentation, the pH remained close to the initial value of 5.5. 
Compared with that on the first day, the pH of each experimental group 
on Day 6 did not significantly change, and the p value ranged from 0.496 
to 1. The pH of the air treatment group increased to 7.16 on the 8th day,

and this value was maintained. However, the N2 and CK experimental 
groups exhibited growth on Day 10 and began to stabilize at a pH of 
approximately 7 on Day 12. In lactate-driven CE reactions, the pH varies 
in the range of 5–7. Montecchio et al. reported that the most suitable pH 
for lactate elongation was 6 (Montecchio et al., 2024). Our results 
showed some discrepancies, but the optimal pH range was close to the 
reported optimal pH range. This observation may be attributed to the 
enrichment of CE microorganisms, altering the chemical environment of 
the AD system during the CE process. 
The ammonia nitrogen concentration has an effect on CE bacteria, 
and a high ammonia nitrogen concentration (2.1 g/L) inhibits MCCAs 
synthesis (Zhang et al., 2019). The ammonia nitrogen concentration 
during the AD process of each experimental group is illustrated in 
Fig. 4g. The Air experimental group exhibited ammonia nitrogen

concentration ranging from 600 to 800 mg/L, whereas the H2 treatment 
group exhibited ammonia nitrogen concentration ranging from 500 to 
850 mg/L. The N2 and CK experimental groups showed peak nitrogen 
levels of 1469 and 1513 mg/L, respectively, taking ten days to achieve 
relative stability. The N2 and CK treatments had adverse effects on the 
CE process and outcome. The lower ammonia concentration in the Air 
experimental group suggests that Air-NBW also has the effect of 
reducing ammonia nitrogen in the AD system for the production of 
MCCAs, maintaining the CE bacteria in a suitable ammonia nitrogen 
environment. The decrease in ammonia nitrogen concentration 
observed with Air-NBW is potentially associated with the heightened 
activity of anaerobic bacteria. During the production of MCCAs, 
anaerobic bacteria utilize ammonia nitrogen as a nitrogen source for 
cellular activities (Jiang et al., 2019). The highest MCCAs yield was 
correlated with increased anaerobic bacterial activity, consequently 
leading to greater consumption of ammonia nitrogen. 
Lactate-based CE relies on LDH to oxidize lactate to pyruvate and 
further react with acetyl coenzyme A (Kim et al., 2022); thus, LDH can 
respond to the effect of different NBWs on lactate oxidation. The LDH 
concentrations are shown in Fig. 4h. The LDH concentration of the Air 
experimental group was 64.35 U/mL, which was 58.03 % greater than 
that of the CK experimental group (40.72 U/mL). The concentration in 
the H2 experimental group was 50.00 U/mL, which was 22.79 % greater 
than that in the CK experimental group. At 39.41 U/mL, the concen­
tration in the N2 experimental group was slightly lower than that in the 
CK experimental group. The LDH concentration among the experimental 
groups and the peak MCCAs concentrations exhibited high consistency. 
This finding implies that Air-NBW increased LDH activity in AD, 
hastened the oxidation of the electron donor lactate, accelerated the 
production of acetyl coenzyme A, and accelerated the CE reaction. 
EPS can serve as an energy source for microorganisms, and EPS 
proteins possess electrochemically active compounds that facilitate 
electron transfer between bacteria (Song et al., 2017). As shown in 
Fig. 4i-j, EPS consisted predominantly of proteins and polysaccharides, 
with protein being the key component, indicating that Air-NBW notably 
stimulated proteins secretion in EPS. The Air experimental group 
exhibited the highest levels of protein and polysaccharides, with protein 
mainly accumulating in LB-EPS at a concentration of 395.09 μg/mL, 
exhibiting a 57.26 % increase from that of the CK experiment group 
(251.23 μg/mL). The LB-EPS of the Air experimental group had a 
polysaccharide concentration of 176.59 μg/mL, indicating a 23.85 % 
increase compared to that of the CK experimental group, which had a 
concentration of 142.85 μg/mL. Wang et al. reported that the addition of 
iron oxide increased the secretion of electroactive EPS, stimulated 
ethanol oxidation and facilitated electron transfer by CE bacteria (Wang 
et al., 2023c). In t this study, an increase in proteins and polysaccharides 
were incorporated into EPS. Protein was identified as the main 
component of EPS, which could create a conducive microbial environ­
ment for lactate oxidation and CE. 
The ORP in the AD system impacts microorganism growth in the 
reactor. A lower ORP indicates more strict anaerobic conditions (Xu 
et al., 2014). The ORP in the NBW experimental group was greater than 
that in the CK experimental group (Fig. S2), suggesting that the addition 
of NBW affected the anaerobic environment. The ORP of the Air 
experimental group was the highest and was significantly greater than 
that of the CK experimental group (p < 0.05). However, no significant

3.3. Understanding the impacts of nanobubble water on the electron 
transfer efficiency 
CE is primarily facilitated through electron transfer between the 
electron donor and electron acceptor for completion of the redox reac­
tion. A high electron transfer efficiency accelerates the CE reaction; thus, 
the electron transfer efficiency of the AD system was examined to assess 
the CE efficiency. Fig. 5a presents the CV curves from all experiments, 
demonstrating that the inclusion of NBW in the experimental group 
resulted in reduction peaks. Notably, the Air experimental group dis­
played the largest reduction peak current, followed by the H2 experi­
mental group and the N2 experimental group, and the smallest reduction 
peak current was observed in the CK experimental group. The CV curves 
show exhibit the extracellular electron transfer capacity and the corre­
lation between electroactive microorganisms in the AD system (Feng 
et al., 2018). A comparison of the CV curve outcomes indicates that the 
incorporation of NBW enhances the electrochemical activity of the AD 
system. 
The EIS curves for each experimental group are shown in Fig. 5b. The 
slope of the curve in the low-frequency region of the Nyquist curve 
provides insight into the resistance of the electrolyte. The higher the 
slope is, the greater the resistance (Choi et al., 2017). The slope of the CK 
experimental group was the greatest, followed by that of the N2 exper­
imental group. The slope of the H2 experimental group was reduced 
compared with that of the N2 experimental group but greater than that 
of the Air experimental group. The slope of the Air experimental group 
was the smallest, resulting in a lower electron transfer resistance, which 
is beneficial for enhancing the electron transfer efficiency. 
Fig. S3 displays the I-t curves of various experimental groups at a 
constant voltage. The EDC and EAC are calculated by integrating the 
current curves under applied constant positive and negative voltages. 
The EAC and EDC were consequently calculated by integrating the 
current curves (Fig. 5c). The EAC and EDC of the Air experimental group 
were 178.55 and 30.66 μmol/g C, respectively. In contrast, the EAC and 
EDC of the CK experimental group were 119.11 and 113.46 μmol/g C, 
respectively. The addition of Air-NBW significantly enhanced the EAC 
(p < 0.05) while reducing the EDC (p < 0.05). The H2 and N2 experi­
mental groups displayed similar increases in the EAC and decreases in 
the EDC, suggesting that the addition of NBW is favourable for 
enhancing the reduction potential of the AD system. This study also 
examined, for the first time, the effect of NBW on the EAC and EDC of the 
MCCAs system used to produce AD. 
After the addition of NBW, the ETS activity in all three experimental 
groups surpassed that in the CK group (Fig. 5d). The Air experimental 
group demonstrated the highest ETS activity (98.88 mg/g-h), which 
exceeded that of the CK experimental group by 40.75 %. The ETS ac­
tivities of the H2 experimental group (82.36 mg/g-h) and the N2 
experimental group (80.25 mg/g-h) exceeded those of the CK experi­
mental group by 17.24 % and 14.23 %, respectively. The inclusion of 
NBW considerably enhanced the ETS activity of the AD system, where 
Air-NBW exhibited the most favorable impact. ETS activity characterizes 
the electron transfer activity of AD systems and microbial activity (Yin

3.4. Understanding the impact of NBW on cow manure degradation 
The AD efficiency of cow manure is limited by the presence of 
components such as lignin, which are difficult to decompose. Evaluating 
the degradation level of the fermentation substrate, namely, cow 
manure, plays a crucial role in obtaining a better understanding of this 
mechanism. XPS was employed to characterize the chemical composi­
tion of the carbon in the digestate at the end of AD (Fig. 6a). Here, the 
C1s spectrum is separated into three peaks: peak 1 represents C-C, which 
is primarily derived from hydrocarbon organics such as polysaccharides; 
peak 2 embodies C-O and C-N; and peak 3 corresponds to COOR (Yin 
et al., 2015). Among all the experimental groups, peak 1 had the highest 
percentage, with 54.13 % in the Air experimental group, 61.4 % in the 
H2 experimental group, 62.27 % in the N2 experimental group, and 
79.42 % in the CK experimental group. The addition of NBW noticeably 
decreased the area share of peak 1. Yu et al. analyzed the rupture of 
surface C-C resulting in the conversion of lignin from solid to liquid (Yu 
et al., 2022). That is, NBW assists in the breakdown of lignin in cow 
manure. 
The EEM spectra (Fig. 6b) can indicate alterations in organic com­
pounds within DOM (Song et al., 2023). The inclusion of Air-NBW 
resulted in a substantial increase in the humic acid levels within the 
DOM. This points towards increased degradation of organic matter 
present in the substrate. As it contains numerous oxygen-containing 
functional groups that transfer electrons within the AD system, humic 
acid plays a critical role in promoting the breakdown of complex sub­
strates in anaerobic environments (Zhao et al., 2023). The higher humic 
acid content of the Air experimental group corresponded to its highest 
MCCAs concentrations and electron transfer efficiency. 
XRD analysis was conducted on both the DOM and digestate 
(Fig. 6c). The diffraction peaks consistently appeared at 2-θ in all the 
experimental groups, indicating similar crystal structures. The DOM and 
air in the digestate experimental groups exhibited the lowest crystal­
linity, whereas those in the CK experimental group had the highest 
crystallinity. The low degree of crystallinity indicates that the structural 
integrity of the substance’s crystals has been compromised (Olatunji and 
Madyira, 2023). Furthermore, the introduction of NBW amplifies the 
disturbance of the crystal structure of the organic matter. 
The differences in the functional groups of the DOM and digestate 
were examined using FTIR (Fig. 6d). Two noteworthy characteristic

3.5. Microbial analysis 
To elucidate the mechanism of action of NBW, we evaluated the 
microbial community in each experimental group during AD (Fig. 7). 
The highest proportion of Firmicutes was observed in all the experi­
mental groups at the phylum level (Fig. 7a). However, NBW did not have 
a notable impact on Firmicutes, which is recognized for breaking down 
complex organic matter, and most CE microorganisms are classified as 
Firmicutes (Wu et al., 2018). The relative abundances of Actinobacteria 
in the Air experimental group, H2 experimental group, N2 experimental 
group and CK experimental group were 5.76, 6.26, 6.06 and 5.19 %, 
respectively. The promotion of MCCAs production by Actinobacteriota 
is achieved through the release of extracellular enzymes that decompose 
organic matter macromolecules into VFAs (Zhang et al., 2023). The 
abundance of Bacteroidota was 7.26 % in the Air experimental group, 
6.65 % in the H2 experimental group, and 4.89 % in the N2 experimental 
group. These values were 113.53, 95.59, and 43.82 % higher, respec­
tively, than those in the CK experimental group (3.40 %). The phylum 
Bacteroides represents a phylum in the CE system comprising organic 
degrading bacteria, and this phylum plays a vital function in MCCAs 
production (Wang et al., 2023a). Compared with the CK experimental 
group (0.91 %), the relative abundances of Halobacterota in the Air, H2, 
and N2 experimental groups were 2.72, 5.93, and 2.13 %, respectively. 
These values were 198.90, 551.65, and 134.07 % greater than those of 
the CK experimental group. In AD, the Halobacterota phylum is involved 
in cellulose degradation (Yang et al., 2023). The better substrate 
degradation in the NBW experimental group was associated with its 
increased relative abundance. 
At the genus level (Fig. 7b), the relative abundance of Bacillus was 
significantly increased by NBW addition, representing 19.21, 43.15, and 
24.95 % of bacterial genera in the air, H2, and N2 experimental groups 
(p < 0.05), respectively, and these values were 135, 428, and 20 % 
greater than that of the CK experimental group (8.18 %). It has been 
reported that Bacillus is involved in the production of MCCAs, and the 
increase in its relative abundance contributes to MCCAs synthesis (Wu 
et al., 2022a). Caproiciproducens is a typical genus of caproic acid- 
producing bacteria that produces caproic acid using lactic acid as an 
electron donor (Tang et al., 2022). Caproiciproducens was present in all 
the experimental groups, with the highest relative abundance of 3.99 % 
in the Air experimental group, which was slightly greater than the 3.93 
% in the CK experimental group. Lactobacillus degrades organic matter 
to produce lactic acid for CE, which is related to MCCAs production 
(Kurniawan et al., 2023). The relative abundance of bacteria in the air 
experimental group was 2.48 %, which was greater than that in the CK 
experimental group (1.78 %). In the AD system, Syntrophomonas enables 
electron transfer between different bacteria (Zhao et al., 2018), and the 
relative abundance in the Air experimental group was 2.25 %, which 
was 70.45 % greater than that in the CK experimental group (1.32 %). 
Tax4 Fun predicted the metabolic functions of microbial commu­
nities following the introduction of various NBW (Fig. S4). The 
enhancement of carbohydrate metabolism, amino acid metabolism and 
membrane transport metabolic pathways suggested that the addition of 
Air-NBW enhanced the degradation of CM and provided more substrates 
for CE. This analysis further revealed that the relative abundance of ABC 
transporters (9.30 %) was significantly (p < 0.05) greater in the Air 
experimental group than in the CK experimental group (7.96 %), and an 
increase in the relative abundance of ABC transporters enhances AD 
microbial activity and promotes hemicellulose degradation (Zhang 
et al., 2022a). We also analysed the expression of key enzyme-encoding 
genes involved in the CE reaction in the Air experimental group and the 
control group (Fig. S4d). The relative abundance of genes related to the 
RBO pathway decreased, whereas the relative abundance of genes 
related to the FAB pathway (6.4.1.2) increased. The abundance in the 
Air experimental group was 0.3637 %, which was 11.66 % greater than 
that in the control group. The addition of NBW simultaneously promotes 
FAB and carbohydrate metabolism, resulting in increased MCCAs pro­
duction potential (Yu et al., 2023). 
3.6. Implications 
This study presented a promising approach to improve the produc­
tion of MCCAs from cow manure AD by adding NBW. The results 
demonstrated that Air-NBW had a significant impact on increasing 
MCCAs production, with caproic acid concentration reaching 15.10 g/L, 
which is 55.03 % greater than that of the CK experimental group. Cor­
relation analysis was performed based on the changes in key physico­
chemical properties and MCCAs concentrations during the AD process 
(Fig. 8a). A positive correlation was noted between the caproic acid 
concentration and the EAC and LDH and a negative correlation was 
noted between the caproic acid concentration and the lactic acid con­
centration. Consequently, it is plausible that the higher caproic acid 
concentration in the Air experimental group was due to the following 
relationships (Fig. 8b): (1) Air-NBW enhanced the electron transfer ca­
pacity of the AD system, accelerating the redox reaction of the CE pro­
cess; (2) Air-NBW facilitated the decomposition of recalcitrant organic 
matter in cow manure, leading to an improved substrate utilization rate;

(3) Air-NBW decreased the ammonia nitrogen concentration in the AD 
system, thereby maintaining it in a favorable ammonia-nitrogen envi­
ronment; (4) Air-NBW boosted the abundance of CE-related Caproici­
producens for MCCAs synthesis; (5) the increase in the abundance of the 
commensal bacterium Syntrophomonas and the increase in electron 
transfer capacity enhanced the efficiency of electron transfer between 
different bacteria, improving reaction activities; and (6) the enhance­
ment of FAB metabolic pathways, carbohydrate metabolism, and ABC 
transporters promoted cow manure degradation and increased the 
production potential of MCCAs. 
The introduction of Air-NBW altered the microbial community 
structure, increasing the relative abundance of microorganisms associ­
ated with MCCAs production and enhancing electron transfer among 
different bacteria, thereby enhancing the carbohydrate metabolism 
pathway. Microorganisms employ exogenous and endogenous mecha­
nisms for survival in diverse environments, perceiving changes in 
chemical gradients and evolving towards conditions conducive to mi­
crobial growth through a phenomenon known as chemotaxis (Fang 
et al., 2024; Miller et al., 2009). NBW directly disrupts the structure of 
recalcitrant organic compounds such as lignocellulose, facilitating 
degradation by hydrolytic bacteria. Additionally, prior to rupture, NBW 
facilitates electron transfer, enhancing interspecies electron transfer 
among microorganisms and the activity of electron transfer systems. 
These effects of NBW induce changes in the chemical environment of AD 
systems. The chemotaxis of anaerobic bacteria prompts functional mi­
croorganisms to demonstrate an enhanced adaptive capacity for sub­
strate degradation and MCCAs production. 
4. Conclusion 
In this study, we evaluated the effect of different types (air, H2, and 
N2) of NBW on MCCAs production from cow manure AD. Air-NBW had 
the best effect, with caproic acid concentration reaching 15.10 g/L, 
which was 55.03 % greater than that of the CK experimental group. Air- 
NBW enhanced electron transfer and substrate degradation and reduced 
ammonia nitrogen. This process stimulates changes in the structure of
